stages.name: Exchange rate systems
stages.title: Exchange rate systems
stages.sub: How exchange rates are set, and how they affect trade and the current account.

steps.q: Lots of people want to buy pounds today, but few people want to sell them. In an open market with no government involved, what happens to the price of the pound?
steps.right: It rises, because demand exceeds supply
steps.wrong: It stays the same, because only the government can move it
steps.hint: Think about any market: if buyers outnumber sellers at the current price, what does the price do?

steps.q: A government decides never to intervene, so that price you just worked out is left to move purely with demand and supply, day to day. What kind of system is this?
steps.right: One where the market alone sets the rate
steps.wrong: One where the government sets the rate
steps.hint: If nobody steps in to hold the price still, who is actually deciding it?

steps.q: The pound falls in value, so UK goods become cheaper for foreign buyers and foreign goods become more expensive for UK buyers. What is likely to happen to UK exports and imports?
steps.hint: If UK goods are now cheaper abroad, do foreigners buy more or less of them?

steps.q: The pound is trading well above the level demand and supply would normally give it, so UK exports look expensive abroad and imports look cheap at home. What does this do to the gap between what the UK earns from exports and spends on imports?
steps.right: It widens the gap, with more spent on imports than earned from exports
steps.wrong: It closes the gap, balancing exports and imports

steps.q: A country's central bank announces the currency will always be exchanged at exactly 5 units per dollar, and it will buy or sell its own currency to keep it there. Can the price of this currency move with demand and supply?
steps.right: No, it is held at the announced level
steps.wrong: Yes, it still moves freely each day
steps.hint: If the bank always intervenes to hold the rate at one number, can the market push it elsewhere?

steps.q: A central bank normally lets its currency move with demand and supply, but occasionally buys or sells it to stop sharp swings. Is this the same as always fixing it at one level, or always leaving it alone?
steps.right: Neither, it mostly floats but is sometimes steered
steps.wrong: It is the same as always fixing it at one level
steps.hint: The bank does not announce one fixed number, but it does not always stay hands-off either.
